title: Three kinds of reading
hookLine: unbroken, continuous, and the slow sehaj path at your own pace

lines: A MARATHON, OR A GARDEN WALK.
FROM ONE HYMN TO THE WHOLE GRANTH.
cards: A long book can be read the way a marathon is run, or the way a garden is walked. Some people sprint the last chapters at two in the morning because they can't stop.
Others leave a bookmark in for a season and come back to it on Sundays. Both finish. They just meet different books along the way.
So how do Sikhs read the whole Guru Granth Sahib, from its first page to its last? There's more than one pace for it, and each one has a name.

teach.b: A path, in Punjabi, is a reading. The first pace is the akhand path.
Akhand means unbroken. The whole Granth is read aloud from start to finish without a single pause, by a team of readers taking turns, one handing the line to the next so the voice never stops.
Families hold one for a wedding, a birth, a death, a new house, or a hard time. The code speaks to how it should be done: clearly, carefully, with attention, never as background noise.
The second pace keeps the reading going in order across set sittings, day after day, so that it finishes in time for an occasion.

teach.h: IN ORDER, WITH RESTS, OR WITH NO CLOCK.
teach.b: Continuous, but with rests. And the third is the sehaj path. It has no clock at all.
You read the Granth in order, at your own pace, a page or a hymn at a sitting, and you pick up where you stopped. One person can do it alone at home, in whatever time life allows. Now the word sehaj.
In Gurbani it names poise, ease, a settled balance of the mind, the calm that comes when a person stops fighting the hukam. So the slow reading is named for the state it hopes to grow.
You don't read the Granth fast in order to reach sehaj. You read it in sehaj.
And it fits this stretch of the path: rising early, the sangat, the gurdwara's order, the Granth opened and rested, the words that may be sung, the hukam. Each one was about how the word is received.
The sehaj path says it can be received at a walking pace too.

how: Sikh families arrange an akhand path, read without a break by a team of readers, for weddings, births, deaths and other occasions; others keep a sehaj path at home, reading the Granth in order at their own pace.

games.q: you want to read the whole Granth, but you have a job, a family and a few quiet minutes a day. which reading fits?
o: an akhand path, alone, without stopping.
a sehaj path, in order, at your own pace.
none; wait until life is quieter.
games.why: the sehaj path is made for this: one person, in order, as much as a sitting allows, picking up where you stopped.

practice: Choose a text that matters to you, the Granth if it's yours, or any book you've meant to read properly, and be honest about how much you could read at one sitting without rushing: a page, a hymn, a paragraph.
Picture where you'd sit, and the bookmark going in at the end of the first sitting.

wordCard.voice: Sehaj path. A reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, in order, at your own pace, named for sehaj, poise and settled ease. Today's word.
